# Intake — Battleship

## Requested outcomes and boundaries

- A Node.js HTTP server in "'`server.js` serves a small, single-player Battleship game. It listens on `PORT`, defaulting to 3000; the repository must have no npm runtime or development dependencies.
- `GET /` serves a playable page with document title `Battleship`, a 10×10 target grid, and controls/results that let the player fire at the computer'"'s fleet.
- "'`GET /api/new` creates a game and returns its id. `POST /api/fire` accepts `{ game, row, col }` and returns a `result` in `miss | hit | sunk`; `gameOver` becomes true when all ships are sunk.
- Ship placement and game rules live in a module used by the server. Rule tests live under `test/` and run with `node --test`.
- No particular hosting account or external deployment target is named. The requested consumer surface is the local HTTP server and its browser page.

## Actor, identity, state, and visibility defaults

- Actor: one anonymous player in a browser; authentication and user profiles are out of scope.
- Identity: the server-generated game id identifies the game. A client must retain that id between API calls. No browser cookie or user identity is required; possession of an id is sufficient to act on that game.
- State: each id owns an independent game in server memory. State lasts until the server process exits or the game is replaced; restarting the server loses active games. There is no cross-game shared board or persistence requirement.
- Information boundary: computer ship coordinates stay server-side. The browser sees only the board and outcomes of its own shots, including enough sunk information to play; there is no opponent-facing view.
- Working defaults for discovery/spec to verify: use the conventional five-ship lengths 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, placed straight and without overlap; ships may touch. New games use independent random placements. Repeated shots are rejected without changing state; invalid coordinates and unknown game ids return client errors; shots after game over are rejected. These choices keep the HTTP contract deterministic without adding accounts or persistence.

## Consumer and delivery boundary

The game becomes usable when the returned project is run with `node server.js` and opened at `http://localhost:<PORT>/` (or `http://localhost:3000/` by default). The APIs are available on that same origin. The isolated candidate is not in the original checkout while work proceeds; ShipLoop'"'s guarded final return makes the source checkout reflect the reviewed result. No hosted deployment or publication is requested.

## Open questions assigned to discovery

- Confirm the installed Node version and built-in "'`node:test` support; this gates the executable test route and compatibility claim.
- Confirm whether a repo-provided constraint, platform limitation, or usable browser check changes the assumed HTML delivery, server lifetime, or game contract; the starting repository is empty and has no documented constraints.
- Refine exact API failure status/body behavior and repeat-shot handling into testable rules; current default is HTTP 400 for malformed/out-of-range/repeated shots, HTTP 404 for unknown game ids, and HTTP 409 after game over.

No user decision blocks intake: each unresolved detail has a conservative local default and discovery can inspect the actual environment before planning.
EOF

## Requested outcomes and boundaries

- A Node.js HTTP server in "'`server.js` serves a small, single-player Battleship game. It listens on `PORT`, defaulting to 3000; the repository must have no npm runtime or development dependencies.

## Actor, identity, state, and visibility defaults

- Actor: one anonymous player in a browser; authentication and user profiles are out of scope.
- Identity: the server-generated game id identifies the game. A client must retain that id between API calls. No browser cookie or user identity is required; possession of an id is sufficient to act on that game.
- State: each id owns an independent game in server memory. State lasts until the server process exits or the game is replaced; restarting the server loses active games. There is no cross-game shared board or persistence requirement.
- Information boundary: computer ship coordinates stay server-side. The browser sees only the board and outcomes of its own shots, including enough sunk information to play; there is no opponent-facing view.
- Working defaults for discovery/spec to verify: use the conventional five-ship lengths 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, placed straight and without overlap; ships may touch. New games use independent random placements. Repeated shots are rejected without changing state; invalid coordinates and unknown game ids return client errors; shots after game over are rejected. These choices keep the HTTP contract deterministic without adding accounts or persistence.

## Consumer and delivery boundary

The game becomes usable when the returned project is run with `node server.js` and opened at `http://localhost:<PORT>/` (or `http://localhost:3000/` by default). The APIs are available on that same origin.
